title: The fig tree and the temple (Mark 11:12–19)
hook: Mark sandwiches a barren fig tree around the temple scene: a house of prayer for all nations
carry: a house of prayer for all

segments.voice: Yesterday, a borrowed colt, Hosanna, and your line was the lord has need of it. What did you lend? Day two hundred seven.

The next morning, walking in from Bethany, Jesus is hungry. Far off he sees a fig tree in full leaf, and goes to see if there's anything on it. Nothing. Only leaves. And then Mark adds a short line that readers keep tripping over: "for the time of figs was not yet." It wasn't even the season. And Jesus speaks to the tree: no one will ever eat fruit from you again. And, Mark says, his disciples heard it. Fruit out of season? It's a fair question to ask of the story. Hold on to that puzzle. Mark is a storyteller who likes to make sandwiches: he starts one story, cuts into the middle of it with another, and then finishes the first. The fig tree is the bread. Here comes the filling.
screen: `HUNGRY, AND A FIG TREE.` → `ONLY LEAVES. NOT THE SEASON.` → `A MARK SANDWICH.`

segments.voice: They come into Jerusalem, and Jesus goes into the temple courts and starts throwing people out, the buyers and the sellers. He overturns the tables of the money changers and the seats of the people selling doves. In the Law of Moses, doves were the offering for someone who couldn't afford a lamb. And Mark adds that he wouldn't let anyone carry goods through the temple, as if it were a shortcut. Then he teaches, with two old prophets in his mouth. In the King James Bible: "Is it not written, My house shall be called of all nations the house of prayer? but ye have made it a den of thieves." The first half is Isaiah: a house of prayer for all nations, foreigners included. Matthew and Luke, telling the same scene, leave out those words, of all nations. Mark keeps them. Some readers think the trading filled the outer court, where people who weren't Jewish could come to pray. The second half is Jeremiah. A den of thieves isn't where robbers rob. It's the hideout they run back to, to feel safe. Jesus is standing where Israel's prophets stood, speaking from inside his own tradition about his own temple. The chief priests and scribes hear, and start looking for a way to destroy him, because the crowds are spellbound. And now back to the bread: the fig tree. Some readers see it as a sign acted out, a picture of the temple scene. Plenty of leaves, lots of activity, and no fruit. Mark doesn't explain; he sets them side by side and lets us look.
screen: `TABLES AND DOVES OVERTURNED.` · `ISAIAH: FOR ALL NATIONS.` · `JEREMIAH: A ROBBERS' HIDEOUT.` · `LEAVES, BUT NO FRUIT.` · then, large: `MY HOUSE SHALL BE CALLED OF ALL NATIONS THE HOUSE OF PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: widen the circle. Settle, and breathe. Picture a map of the world, and let your attention travel slowly across it. Your own town. Your country. A place in the news this week. A place you've never thought about at all. Imagine all of them welcome in one house of prayer. If you pray, you can pray for the nations, one place at a time, by name. If you don't, simply wish each place well as you pass over it. The bell holds the time.
Isaiah, the prophet whose words Jesus quotes: my house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations. A tree with leaves and no fruit, wrapped around that very house.
Your line: a house of prayer for all. Today, notice who's missing from the places you gather, and make room for one of them. Day two hundred seven.

howItsDone: Some churches pray for the nations of the world in their weekly prayers, and the temple scene is often read during Holy Week, remembering Jesus's words that God's house is for all people.

fork.setup: you walk into the temple courts in Jerusalem. tables of coins, cages of doves, people cutting through with goods. what does Jesus do?
options: find a quiet corner to pray.
pay the temple tax and leave.
fork.reveal: he overturns the tables and the dove-sellers' seats, and quotes Isaiah and Jeremiah: a house of prayer for all nations.

original.note: Greek: a cave, a den. in Mark 11:17, a cave of robbers, echoing Jeremiah 7:11.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus lost his temper in church.
what it means: a prophet's act inside his own tradition, calling the temple back to being a house of prayer for everyone.
what a scholar hears: Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11 in one breath, and a fig-tree sandwich, a way Mark uses more than once to make two stories explain each other.

sources.ref: Mark 11:12–19; Isaiah 56:7; Jeremiah 7:11; Leviticus 5:7; Matthew 21:13; Luke 19:46

notes: Care taken to frame the temple action as prophetic critique from within Judaism, not a rejection of Judaism or the Jewish people. Keeper to confirm tone.
Money changers and the Tyrian shekel for the temple tax; doves as the offering of the poor (Leviticus 5:7; 12:8). Confirm.
'Many scholars think the trading filled the outer court' (the Court of the Gentiles). Confirm.
'Mark is the only gospel that keeps of all nations' (Matthew 21:13 and Luke 19:46 omit). Confirm.
Sandwich (intercalation) as a Markan technique is widely noted.
